questions.stem: An object moves in a circle at constant speed. In which direction is its acceleration?
options: There is none, because the speed is constant
Towards the centre of the circle
Along the tangent, in the direction of motion
Away from the centre of the circle
questions.explanation: In uniform circular motion the speed is constant but the direction of the velocity keeps changing, so the object accelerates. The acceleration is perpendicular to the velocity, directed towards the centre: centripetal acceleration.

questions.stem: Vectors are drawn for an object's velocity a moment apart as it moves around a circle at constant speed. In which direction does Δv = v(final) − v(initial) point?
options: Along the tangent, in the direction of motion
Away from the centre of the circle
Along the tangent, opposite to the motion
Towards the centre of the circle
questions.explanation: Subtracting the initial velocity vector from the final one, for a very short time interval, gives a Δv perpendicular to the velocity and pointing towards the centre. Because a = Δv/Δt, the acceleration also points towards the centre.

questions.stem: A car travels at 15 m s⁻¹ around a flat curve of radius 50 m. What is its centripetal acceleration?
options: 11 m s⁻²
4.5 m s⁻²
3.3 m s⁻²
questions.explanation: a = v²/r = 15²/50 = 225/50 = 4.5 m s⁻². Dividing v by r without squaring gives 0.30 m s⁻².

questions.stem: The 1200 kg car on the flat 50 m curve at 15 m s⁻¹ needs a centripetal acceleration of 4.5 m s⁻². What force provides this, and how large is it?
options: The car's engine, pushing outwards, 5.4 × 10³ N
Friction between the tyres and the road, 2.7 × 10² N
The normal force from the road, 1.2 × 10⁴ N
Friction between the tyres and the road, 5.4 × 10³ N
questions.explanation: On a flat curve, sideways friction between tyres and road provides the centripetal force: F = ma = 1200 × 4.5 = 5.4 × 10³ N, towards the centre. The normal force is vertical, so on a flat road it cannot provide a horizontal force.

questions.stem: A ball on a string moves in a horizontal circle of radius 0.80 m, completing one revolution every 0.50 s. What is its speed?
options: 3.2 m s⁻¹
10 m s⁻¹
1.6 m s⁻¹
5.0 m s⁻¹
questions.explanation: v = 2πr/T = 2π × 0.80/0.50 = 10 m s⁻¹. Dividing r by T without the 2π gives 1.6 m s⁻¹, which is the radius covered per second rather than the circumference.

questions.stem: A ball on a string moves in a circle of radius 0.80 m with a period of 0.50 s. What is its centripetal acceleration?
options: 63 m s⁻²
126 m s⁻²
10 m s⁻²
20 m s⁻²
questions.explanation: v = 2πr/T = 10.05 m s⁻¹, so a = v²/r = 10.05²/0.80 ≈ 126 m s⁻². Equivalently a = 4π²r/T². The 10 m s⁻¹ is the speed, not the acceleration.

questions.stem: A 0.20 kg puck on a frictionless table moves in a circle of radius 0.60 m at 3.0 m s⁻¹, held by a string to a central pin. What is the tension in the string?
questions.explanation: The tension is the only horizontal force, so it provides the centripetal force: F = mv²/r = 0.20 × 3.0²/0.60 = 3.0 N. Using v instead of v² gives 1.0 N.

questions.stem: A car's speed around a curve of fixed radius is doubled. What happens to the centripetal force needed?
options: It becomes half as large
It becomes four times as large
It becomes twice as large
It stays the same, because the radius is fixed
questions.explanation: F = mv²/r, so the force is proportional to the square of the speed. Doubling the speed needs four times the force, which is why speeding on curves is so dangerous.

questions.stem: A ball whirled in a horizontal circle on a string is released when the string breaks. How does it move, seen from above?
options: Straight inwards, towards the centre of the circle
In a straight line along the tangent at the point of release
Straight outwards, away from the centre of the circle
In a curve that continues around the original circle
questions.explanation: Once the string breaks, there is no centripetal force, so by Newton's first law the ball continues with its velocity at that instant, which is along the tangent. There is no outward force throwing it away from the centre.

questions.stem: Why is it dangerous to take a flat curve at speed on an icy road?
options: Ice makes the normal force point outwards, pushing the car off the road
Ice increases the radius of the curve, so the car cannot follow it
Ice reduces the friction that must provide the centripetal force
Ice increases the car's mass, so it needs a larger centripetal force
questions.explanation: On a flat curve only friction can provide the horizontal force towards the centre. On ice the maximum friction is small, so it may be less than mv²/r, and the car slides outwards along a straighter path.

questions.stem: How does banking a curve reduce the need for friction?
options: The car's weight tilts, so its horizontal component points towards the centre
The normal force becomes larger than the weight and pushes the car outwards
The car's weight decreases on the slope, so less centripetal force is needed
The normal force tilts, so its horizontal component points towards the centre
questions.explanation: On a banked road the normal force is perpendicular to the sloping surface, so it has a horizontal component directed towards the centre of the curve. At the design speed this component alone provides the centripetal force. Weight always acts vertically downward.

questions.stem: A car rounds a banked curve at exactly its design speed. Which forces act on the car in the plane of the curve's cross-section?
options: Its weight, the normal force and an outward centrifugal force
Only the normal force, because the weight is balanced by the banking
Its weight, the normal force and friction pointing up the slope
Only its weight and the normal force; no sideways friction is needed
questions.explanation: At the design speed the vertical component of the normal force balances the weight and its horizontal component provides exactly the centripetal force, so no sideways friction is needed. There is no outward centrifugal force in an inertial frame.

questions.stem: How is gravitational field strength g at a point defined?
options: The distance from that point to the centre of the nearest planet
The gravitational force per unit mass on an object at that point
The gravitational force on any object placed at that point
The mass of the body that produces the gravitational field there
questions.explanation: g = F/m, the force per kilogram, in N kg⁻¹. Because F = ma, this is also the acceleration due to gravity at that point, so 1 N kg⁻¹ = 1 m s⁻².

questions.stem: What is the gravitational force between Earth and an 80 kg person on its surface? Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², Earth's mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m.
questions.explanation: F = GMm/r² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴ × 80/(6.37 × 10⁶)² ≈ 785 N, which agrees with mg = 80 × 9.80. Forgetting to square the radius gives about 5.0 × 10⁹ N.

questions.stem: Two objects attract each other with a gravitational force F. Both masses are doubled and the distance between their centres is also doubled. What is the new force?
options: 2F
F
4F
questions.explanation: F ∝ m₁m₂/r². Doubling both masses multiplies the force by 4, and doubling the distance divides it by 2² = 4, so the force is unchanged.

questions.stem: The distance between two masses is tripled. What happens to the gravitational force between them?
options: It becomes nine times as large
It becomes one-ninth as large
It becomes one-third as large
It becomes three times as large
questions.explanation: Newton's law of universal gravitation is an inverse square law, F ∝ 1/r². Tripling r divides the force by 3² = 9.

questions.stem: How does the gravitational force of Earth on the Moon compare with the force of the Moon on Earth?
options: Earth's pull exists, but the Moon exerts no force on Earth
They are equal in size and opposite in direction
Earth's pull is about 81 times larger, because Earth has more mass
The Moon's pull is larger, because the Moon is accelerating more
questions.explanation: By Newton's third law, and from F = Gm₁m₂/r², the forces on the two bodies are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. The Moon accelerates far more only because its mass is much smaller.

questions.stem: Mars has a mass of 6.42 × 10²³ kg and a radius of 3.39 × 10⁶ m. What is the acceleration due to gravity at its surface? Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
questions.explanation: Equating mg with GMm/r² gives g = GM/r² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6.42 × 10²³/(3.39 × 10⁶)² = 3.73 m s⁻². The object's own mass cancels out. Not squaring the radius gives 1.26 × 10⁷ m s⁻².

questions.stem: At Earth's surface g = 9.80 m s⁻². What is g at a height above the surface equal to Earth's radius?
questions.explanation: At that height the distance from Earth's centre is 2r, twice the surface value. Since g ∝ 1/r², g becomes 9.80/4 = 2.45 m s⁻². Halving g, as if it were proportional to 1/r, gives 4.90.

questions.stem: Two 1000 kg spheres have their centres 1.0 m apart. What is the gravitational force between them? Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
questions.explanation: F = Gm₁m₂/r² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1000 × 1000/1.0² = 6.67 × 10⁻⁵ N. Gravitational forces between everyday objects are tiny; they matter only when at least one mass is astronomical.

questions.stem: Why must the centre of a satellite's circular orbit coincide with the centre of Earth?
options: Earth's magnetic field pushes the satellite towards the centre of Earth at all times
The satellite would otherwise be pulled into a straight path by the Sun's gravity
The only force on it, gravity, points to Earth's centre and must provide the centripetal force
The satellite's engines are aimed at Earth's centre to keep it moving around in a circle
questions.explanation: An orbiting satellite moves only under Earth's gravity, which acts towards Earth's centre. For circular motion the net force must point to the centre of the circle, so that centre must be Earth's centre.

questions.stem: Equating GMm/r² with mv²/r for a satellite in a circular orbit gives v = √(GM/r). What does this show about the satellite's speed?
options: It depends on the satellite's mass, so heavier satellites must travel faster
It increases with the orbit radius, so higher satellites travel faster
It depends only on the satellite's mass, not on the orbit radius
It depends only on the orbit radius and the central body's mass, not the satellite's mass
questions.explanation: The satellite's mass m cancels from both sides, so v = √(GM/r) depends only on the central mass M and the orbit radius r. Larger orbits have lower speeds, and a feather and a spacecraft in the same orbit would move together.

questions.stem: The International Space Station orbits about 4.0 × 10⁵ m above Earth's surface. What is its orbital speed? Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻², Earth's mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m.
questions.explanation: The orbit radius is measured from Earth's centre: r = 6.37 × 10⁶ + 4.0 × 10⁵ = 6.77 × 10⁶ m. Then v = √(GM/r) = √(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴/6.77 × 10⁶) = 7.67 × 10³ m s⁻¹. Using the altitude alone as r gives 3.16 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹.

questions.stem: The space station orbits at a radius of 6.77 × 10⁶ m with a speed of 7.67 × 10³ m s⁻¹. What is its period?
options: About 15 minutes
About 24 hours
About 46 minutes
About 92 minutes
questions.explanation: T = 2πr/v = 2π × 6.77 × 10⁶/7.67 × 10³ ≈ 5.55 × 10³ s, about 92 minutes, so the station circles Earth about 15 times a day. Leaving out the factor of 2 gives about 46 minutes.

questions.stem: A satellite is moved from a low circular orbit to a higher one. How do its speed and period change?
options: Its speed decreases and its period decreases
Its speed and period both stay the same
Its speed decreases and its period increases
Its speed increases and its period increases
questions.explanation: From v = √(GM/r), a larger radius gives a lower speed. The satellite also has further to travel, so its period, T = 2πr/v, increases, in line with Kepler's third law.

questions.stem: What does Kepler's first law of planetary motion state?
options: Each planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times
Each planet moves in an ellipse with the Sun at one focus
Each planet moves in a circle with the Sun at the centre
Each planet moves in an ellipse with the Sun at the centre
questions.explanation: Kepler's first law says planetary orbits are ellipses, with the Sun at one of the two foci, not the centre. Equal areas in equal times is the second law.

questions.stem: A comet moves in a long elliptical orbit around the Sun. According to Kepler's second law, where does it move fastest?
options: Furthest from the Sun, because the radius vector sweeps equal areas in equal times
At the same speed everywhere, because the radius vector sweeps equal areas
Halfway between nearest and furthest points, where its path is straightest
Closest to the Sun, because the radius vector sweeps equal areas in equal times
questions.explanation: The line from the Sun to the comet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. Near the Sun the line is short, so the comet must cover a longer arc in the same time to sweep the same area: it moves fastest at its closest point.

questions.stem: Kepler's third law for circular orbits is T² = 4π²r³/GM. Moon P orbits a planet at four times the radius of Moon Q. How do their periods compare?
options: P's period is 8 times Q's
P's period is 4 times Q's
P's period is 16 times Q's
P's period is 64 times Q's
questions.explanation: T² ∝ r³, so T ∝ r^(3/2). Multiplying r by 4 multiplies r³ by 64, so T² is 64 times larger and T is 8 times larger. 64 is the ratio of T², not T.

questions.stem: How is Kepler's third law, T² = 4π²r³/GM, derived for a circular orbit?
options: Set GMm/r² equal to mv and substitute v = r/T
Set GMm/r equal to ½mv² and substitute v = 2πr/T
Set mg equal to mv²/r and substitute g = 9.80 m s⁻²
Set GMm/r² equal to mv²/r and substitute v = 2πr/T
questions.explanation: Gravity provides the centripetal force, GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v² = GM/r. Substituting v = 2πr/T gives 4π²r²/T² = GM/r, which rearranges to T² = 4π²r³/GM.

questions.stem: The Moon orbits Earth at a radius of 3.84 × 10⁸ m with a period of 27.3 days. What mass of Earth does this give? Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
options: 4.5 × 10³⁴ kg
8.0 × 10²² kg
1.6 × 10¹⁷ kg
6.0 × 10²⁴ kg
questions.explanation: M = 4π²r³/(GT²) with T = 27.3 × 86 400 = 2.36 × 10⁶ s, giving M ≈ 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg. Forgetting to convert days to seconds gives a value about 7.5 × 10⁹ times too large.

questions.stem: Earth orbits the Sun at a radius of 1.50 × 10¹¹ m with a period of 3.16 × 10⁷ s. What is the mass of the Sun? Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻².
options: 5.0 × 10²⁸ kg
2.0 × 10³⁰ kg
1.3 × 10¹⁹ kg
6.0 × 10²⁴ kg
questions.explanation: M = 4π²r³/(GT²) = 4π² × (1.50 × 10¹¹)³/(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × (3.16 × 10⁷)²) ≈ 2.0 × 10³⁰ kg. The mass found is that of the central body, the Sun, not of Earth.

questions.stem: A student plots T² against r³ for the moons of Jupiter and gets a straight line through the origin. What is its gradient?
options: 2πr/T, the orbital speed of each moon
4π²/GM, where M is Jupiter's mass
GM/4π², where M is Jupiter's mass
4π²/Gm, where m is the mass of each moon
questions.explanation: Rearranging T² = (4π²/GM)r³ shows T² is proportional to r³ with gradient 4π²/GM, which depends only on the central mass. Measuring the gradient therefore gives Jupiter's mass.

questions.stem: Which statement describes a geostationary satellite's orbit?
options: Over both poles, crossing every part of Earth once a day
Above the equator, opposite to Earth's spin, with a period of 12 hours
At any angle to the equator, with a period of 24 hours
Above the equator, in the direction of Earth's spin, with a period of 24 hours
questions.explanation: A geostationary satellite stays above the same point on the equator. Its orbit must be in the equatorial plane, in the same direction as Earth's rotation, with a period equal to Earth's rotation period.

questions.stem: Why must a geostationary orbit lie in Earth's equatorial plane?
options: Satellites over other latitudes would need to orbit faster than Earth spins to stay above one point
Any orbit is centred on Earth's centre, so a tilted one would drift north and south of the ground point
Only above the equator is Earth's gravity strong enough to hold a satellite with a 24-hour period
Earth's rotation pushes satellites outwards most strongly over the equator, holding them in place
questions.explanation: Every orbit is centred on Earth's centre. A tilted orbit would carry the satellite north of the equator for half of each day and south for the other half, so it could not stay above one point. Only an equatorial orbit stays above a fixed ground point.

questions.stem: What is the radius of a geostationary orbit, with a period of 24.0 hours? Use G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻² and Earth's mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg.
questions.explanation: r³ = GMT²/4π² with T = 8.64 × 10⁴ s gives r ≈ 4.22 × 10⁷ m from Earth's centre. Subtracting Earth's radius gives an altitude of about 3.59 × 10⁷ m, which is the height above the surface, not the orbit radius.

questions.stem: Why are many imaging and mapping satellites placed in low polar orbits?
options: They orbit so fast that they photograph the whole planet in a single pass
They are beyond Earth's gravity, so they need no fuel to stay in orbit
Earth rotates beneath them, so over time they pass over every part of the surface
They stay fixed above one point, so a dish on the ground need not move
questions.explanation: A polar orbit passes over both poles. As Earth rotates underneath, each orbit crosses a different strip, so the satellite eventually views the whole surface, and its low altitude gives detailed images. Staying above one point is what a geostationary orbit does.

questions.stem: How does a geostationary orbit differ from other equatorial orbits?
options: It is the one equatorial orbit whose period matches Earth's rotation
It is the only orbit that lies in the plane of the equator
It is lower than any other equatorial orbit around Earth
It is the only equatorial orbit that is not a circle
questions.explanation: An equatorial orbit is any orbit above the equator, and it can have any radius and period. A geostationary orbit is the particular equatorial orbit at the radius that gives a 24-hour period in the direction of Earth's spin.
